data.title: Airline Norse Atlantic's Norwegian operating unit declares bankruptcy
data.description:
Airline Norse Atlantic's Norwegian operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the long-haul budget carrier said on Friday, succumbing to soaring fuel costs wrought by the war in Iran.

Norse Atlantic ASA, which is listed on the Oslo Euronext Expand bourse, and other group companies are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said in a statement.

Norse Atlantic, which launched in 2022, on Wednesday warned that its financial situation was "critical", and the following day said it had suspended all flights and that the board could file for bankruptcy unless it urgently secured funding.

Earlier on Friday Norse said its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back, a claim contested by the company.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.

"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.

The global aviation industry is suffering its worst crisis since the COVID-19 pandemic as the US-Iran conflict, which began at the end of February, disrupts operations, drives up fuel prices, and sends airlines' costs skyrocketing.

data.title: Croatia Q3 GDP Growth Accelerates To 2.9%
data.description:
BRUSSELS (dpa-AFX) - The Croatian economic growth rebounded in the third quarter, preliminary data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics showed on Friday.

On an unadjusted basis, gross domestic product rose 2.9 percent yearly in the September quarter, following a 1.7 percent growth in the June quarter.

The expenditure breakdown showed that household consumption expenditure grew 2.8 percent, faster than the 0.5 percent increase in the previous quarter. Similarly, the growth in general government consumption accelerated to 4.3 percent from 2.0 percent.

The growth in gross fixed capital formation, or investments, improved to 2.3 percent from 1.5 percent. Meanwhile, net foreign demand was not favorable as exports of goods and services rose only 0.1 percent amid a 9.3 percent surge in imports.

On a quarterly basis, GDP advanced a seasonally adjusted 1.2 percent versus a 0.5 percent increase in the second quarter.

data.title: Euro zone bond yields diverge after choppy week for shares
data.description:
Euro zone bond yields diverged on Friday, as investors returned to equity markets and oil prices were set to snap a three-week losing streak.

After a choppy week for shares, which led many market participants to seek out safe-haven assets such as bonds, Germany's 10-year yield (DE10YT=RR) — the benchmark for the euro zone — rose 1 basis point (bps) to 3.267%. Across the week it was, however, still down by just over 3 bps, its second consecutive weekly decline.

Emerging market stocks were on track for their biggest weekly gain since June, the Europe-wide blue-chip index STOXX 600 was last up about 1%, and Nasdaq and S&P 500 futures rallied 2.2% and 1.6%, respectively.

As a more risk-on environment returned and weighed on demand for bonds, yields were also supported by Thursday's publication of minutes from the European Central Bank's October meeting, which showed that some policymakers were leaning towards an interest rate hike, even as the ECB opted to leave rates unchanged.

Money markets price in two ECB rate increases of 25 bps by June 2027, LSEG data showed.

Brent crude oil futures were up 1.2% as attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure heightened concerns over oil supply from the conflict-hit Middle East.

The two-year German Schatz yield was steady at 3.075%. (DE2YT=RR)

Elsewhere, France's 10-year yield was last down 4.4 bps at 4.699% after official data showed the country's economy contracted more than initially thought in the third quarter. (FR10YT=RR)

The outlook for 2027 remains gloomy, ING analysts said, warning that France's weakening labour market will increasingly weigh on household confidence, income and consumption.

"It is therefore difficult to identify a driver capable of generating a meaningful recovery in domestic demand over the next few quarters ... France will enter next year without economic momentum," the analysts wrote in a note.

S&P is due to review France's rating later on Friday.

Preliminary French and Spanish inflation data for November meanwhile came in below expectations, with flash figures for the wider euro zone due on Tuesday. Economists polled by Reuters were last expecting the headline reading to come in at 3.9% in November, which would be a slight dip from October's 4%.

However, an ECB survey showed euro zone consumers sharply raised their expectation for inflation in the year ahead last month and perceptions also rose significantly, bolstering the case for another interest rate hike.

The spread between French and German yields, a measure of the risk premium attached to France, narrowed to 143 bps, down from a multiyear high of 178 bps it touched on October 22.

Meanwhile, Italy's 10-year bond yield was last down 2 bps at 4.315%.

data.title: US stock selloffs trigger a new kind of dollar bounce
data.description:
Key points:
  • FX hedge rebalancing drives dollar buying after US stock falls
  • Foreign holdings of US equities stood at $25 trillion as of September
  • More volatile markets mean rebalancing is having a bigger impact

By Alun John

An unusual appreciation in the dollar on days after a sharp Wall Street selloff can be explained by shifts in how foreign investors in US stocks protect their portfolios against currency swings, says Citi.

The dollar's jump against a basket of peers on Monday prompted some head-scratching in currency markets, coming against a backdrop of gains in equities, lower Treasury yields and lower oil prices that would typically cause it to depreciate.

The move, says Kristjan Kasikov, Citi's head of FX quant investor solutions, makes sense because it followed Friday's tech-led Wall Street rout, which pushed the S&P 500 into correction territory.

That in turn required dollar buying from asset managers outside the US who own US stocks and have hedges in place to protect against dollar declines.

The fact that such flows can shift the world's most traded currency pairs illustrates how the multi-trillion-dollar overseas holdings of US stocks are shaping world markets, analysts said.

It also reflects ongoing competition between hedge funds trying to profit from trading in advance of FX rebalancing by large equity investors, and those large investors' attempts to trade at the best price.

Investors usually rebalance their portfolios at month end, but some do so more dynamically, normally the day after moves in equities push hedge ratios past preset levels.

Funds hedge by selling dollars in forward markets proportional to the size of their equities holdings. A fall in equities means they need to be less short dollars, and so creates a dollar buying flow.

"Citi’s global real money clients were net dollar buyers on Friday 20th and Monday 23rd, following losses in US equities on prior days. This turned into net dollar selling on Tuesday 24th after US equities bounced on Monday," said Kasikov.

"This behaviour is consistent with continuous or trigger-based FX hedge rebalancing."

FOREIGNERS OWN A LOT OF US STOCKS

There are multiple drivers of the $10-trillion-a-day currency markets, from relative moves in interest rates to shifts in risk sentiment, and many fund managers do not have currency hedges in place.

However, hedging flows have become more important as foreign holdings of US stocks have surged, say analysts.

Foreigners owned around $25 trillion of US equities as of September, according to St Louis Fed data, roughly double the level three years ago due to both inflows and rapid stock market gains.

Foreign flows into US equities have also overtaken flows into relatively more stable Treasuries.

And the latest trend is a result of stock market volatility at a time when these holdings are high.

"I was speaking to one of our FX (portfolio managers), and yesterday we had a big move in US equities, so he's seeing some trigger-based rebalances that are taking place, probably today," said Van Luu, head of FX and fixed income solutions strategy at Russell Investments, speaking last Friday, a day after another Wall Street selloff.

Luu says fund managers' use of dynamic hedging is not new, but "when there's volatility, you will see more rebalancing."

The 4.3% fall in the S&P 500 on November 5 and the 3.7% drop on November 20 were the two biggest daily falls since April 2025.

However, Luu says currency moves on hedge rebalancing are much easier to predict at the end of the month as intra-month changes require making estimates about funds' hedge tolerance bands and positioning.

But that in turn is contributing to a shift towards more immediate changes, said Citi's Kasikov, since these predictable flows are "actively traded by hedge funds", meaning "investors who follow hedged index behaviour and rebalance at month ends are normally the last to trade and may get the worst rate."

To avoid this, he said some investors are shifting to rebalancing their hedges more dynamically, in turn making currency markets more responsive to equity moves.

data.title: Australia clears gas reservation law, industry warns of prolonged uncertainty
data.description:
Key points:
  • Policy sets aside 20% of gas for domestic use from 2028
  • Industry has argued it would deter investment
  • Western Australia, site of major LNG exporters, largely exempt

By Helen Clark and Emily Chow

Australia's domestic gas reservation scheme, which parliament passed on Friday, threatens to prolong market uncertainty as it gives the government broad discretion in how it implements the policy, industry participants said.

The scheme is aimed at resolving a decade of band-aid fixes for high gas prices and threatened supply shortages on Australia's highly populated east coast. The policy requires liquefied natural gas exporters to reserve up to 20% of production for the domestic market from 2028, to achieve a "modest oversupply" equivalent to 110% of forecast demand, targets that can, however, be adjusted by the government based on market conditions.

Australia is the world's No. 2 LNG exporter, mostly supplying northeast Asia, and while the new policy does not apply to existing contracts, some industry players said it would undermine incentives to invest in more supply.

"The policy provides wide-ranging powers to the government to influence the gas market on an ongoing basis," said Saul Kavonic, head of energy research at MST Marquee.

"The policy was intended to rein in gas exporters but in practice may concentrate market power in exporters' hands."

Asian LNG buyers are already grappling with concerns over supply security stemming from the Iran war, which has disrupted around one-fifth of the world's oil and seaborne gas flows.

“Amid ongoing Strait of Hormuz disruptions, (Australia's) policy adds another layer of uncertainty for Asian buyers seeking reliable and diversified LNG supplies,” said Kpler analyst Go Katayama.

Buyers from Japan, a top market for Australian LNG, have already begun diversifying their portfolios to increase US offtake and reduce dependency on Australia.

INVESTMENT ON THE RISE

Australia has grappled for nearly a decade with high gas prices and supply concerns on the east coast, where Origin Energy , Shell and Santos operate LNG export projects that the policy will affect.

Resources Minister Madeleine King told ABC Radio the oversupply mechanism was intended to lower prices, but the government wouldn't set a figure to avoid that figure becoming a price floor.

King said exploration spending was at a 10-year high despite industry concerns the policy would deter gas development.

June quarter investment in energy exploration was up 76.3% from a year earlier to A$584 million ($390 million), Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed.

INDUSTRY OPPOSITION

Industry players have long opposed the new policy, first proposed in 2025, which carries a provision that exporters "must sell" gas locally rather than merely offer it on reasonable terms, as is the case in Western Australia under a scheme that producers have said they prefer.

"It is short-sighted to design a policy that forces a producer to sell its product potentially below the cost of production into a materially oversupplied market," a Shell spokesperson said in a statement on Friday after the lower house of parliament passed the policy.

While Santos' Gladstone LNG project has at times struggled to secure enough gas to meet contracts, the Shell and Origin projects already supply the domestic market, raising concerns among domestic producers that additional volumes could squeeze them out.

The policy largely exempts Western Australia, site of several major LNG projects, because it already operates its own 15% gas reservation policy and is not connected to the east coast gas market.

($1 = 1.4988 Australian dollars)

data.title: UniCredit considers bigger Generali stake among expanded partnership options
data.description:
UniCredit has been weighing a possible increase of its 9% stake in Generali , four people close to the matter said, as Italy's second-biggest bank and the country's largest insurer discuss new commercial accords.

The Generali investment has so far been the only move by UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel in Italy's fast-consolidating banking market.

The veteran dealmaker has just secured control of Germany's Commerzbank , and says UniCredit will grow its domestic market share without any major acquisitions.

Meanwhile, the Generali stake has positioned UniCredit as a counterweight to its main rival Intesa Sanpaolo - which looks set to become the biggest Generali shareholder through a takeover of Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) .

Two of the four people said UniCredit could raise its Generali holding towards the 13.4% stake which is expected to pass from MPS into Intesa's hands.

The outcome of UniCredit's deliberations remains uncertain.

UniCredit and Generali both declined to comment.

By exercising significant influence over Generali, without control, Intesa can book the insurer's profits in its earnings in proportion to the stake, under international accounting rules.

Independent of its Generali stake coming from the MPS deal, Intesa has also built a further 3% stake in the insurer, which it has said it will dispose of.

UniCredit first unveiled a 4.1% Generali stake , before building it up to the current 9.05%. Crossing 10% requires supervisory approval.

UniCredit and Generali, which already partner in eastern Europe, have been discussing closer commercial ties.

On November 9, Orcel said it was up to Generali to decide whether to accept UniCredit's help, adding that he hoped an agreement could be reached in the coming months.

He has repeatedly said such partnerships do not require UniCredit to control Generali, or a formal combination.

Orcel last week put the value of closer cooperation between UniCredit and Generali at €1.5-€2.0 billion ($1.6-$2.2 billion), with Generali remaining independent and simply agreeing to "innovative" forms of partnership.

A day later, Generali CEO Philippe Donnet said the insurer agrees with Orcel's view of the value the two companies can generate together.($1 = 0.9136 euros)

data.title: Thales Enters Exclusive Negotiations For 51.6% Stake In Lumibird
data.description:
NEUILLY-SUR-SEINE (dpa-AFX) - Defense electronics company Thales S.A. (THLEF.PK, HO.PA) announced on Friday that it has entered into exclusive negotiations to acquire a 51.6% stake in laser technology company Lumibird SA (LBIRD.PA) from entities controlled by Chief Executive Officer Marc Le Flohic.

The proposed transaction values Lumibird at 30.10 euros per share, representing a premium of 24.7% to the one-month volume-weighted average share price prior to the announcement, according to Thales.

The company said additional payments of up to 2.56 euros per share could be made if certain conditions linked to the earnout from the planned sale of Lumibird's medical division are met.

Thales said the proposed price implies an enterprise value of about 440 million euros for Lumibird's photonics division.

Following the acquisition of the controlling stake, Thales intends to launch a mandatory simplified tender offer for the remaining Lumibird shares on the same terms and pursue a squeeze-out if the required conditions are met.

The transaction is expected to close by the second quarter of 2027, subject to the disposal of Lumibird's medical division, regulatory approvals and other customary conditions.

Shares of Thales were up 1.88% at 238.20 euros in Paris trading.

On Paris stock exchange, shares of Lumibird were gaining 17.52% at 28.85 euros.

data.title: Bitcoin, Ether Rebound as Markets Stabilize — Update
data.description:
By Joseph Wilkins

Bitcoin rebounded above $61,000 on Friday as Asian markets stabilized and risk appetite returned to cryptocurrencies.

Bitcoin was 1.1% higher at $61,465, while ether gained 1% to $1,720. U.S. stock futures rose Friday following a break for Thanksgiving, with Asian markets taking cues. South Korea's Kospi rose more than 4%, with chip heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics jumping 6.4% and 4.5%, respectively.

Bitcoin's 90-day correlation to the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 has rebuilt since reaching a year-to-date low in September, Block Scholes analyst Thahbib Rahman wrote in a note. Bitcoin's current correlation is 53% to the S&P 500 and 54% to the Nasdaq-100, up from 37% and 36% at the end of October.

Rahman said the flagship cryptocurrency could remain stuck as long as fears around the durability of the AI trade persist and drag down U.S. stocks.

data.title: Trump to meet Abdul El-Sayed on golden ‘TrumpCare’ proposal
data.description:
President Donald Trump has indicated his willingness to meet with Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss the Michigan Democrat’s push to expand Medicare for all Americans, an initiative the latter agreed to rebrand as “TrumpCare.”

“I know I’ll be meeting with him,” Trump said during an interview with The New York Post on Tuesday. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go," he added without specifying the date for the meeting.

Despite Democratic control in Congress, Trump will have to sign, not veto, any proposed legislation on 'Medicare for All,' largely a leftist push to replace private insurance with a publicly funded single-payer national health program.

Championed by progressive Dems such as El-Sayed, 'Medicare for All' represents an area Republicans have long opposed given its potential to increase government spending. Universal healthcare could increase federal subsidies for health care from $1.5T to $3T by 2030, the Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022.

El-Sayed reiterated his push for “Medicare for All” earlier this month, even agreeing to call it “Trumpcare.”

"Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave," he wrote in a social media post with mock images of golden TrumpCare cards attached to get Trump’s attention.

When asked about the golden “TrumpCare” plan, the president called El-Sayed “a smart guy.” “I’m just going to veto everything there is,” he said, adding that healthcare is one area he is willing to negotiate with Democrats on.

“Then at some point I think they’re going to want to negotiate. I will, and we can do health care. We can do a lot of great things together,” Trump said.

data.title: HEG Ltd lists at 25% premium, hits lower circuit
data.description:
Shares of HEG Ltd, formerly HEG Graphite Ltd, debuted on the stock exchanges on Friday at a premium of about 25 per cent, but fell to the 5 per cent lower circuit after listing as investors booked profits.

On the NSE, the stock opened at ₹587, up ₹118.75, or 25.36 per cent, from the pre-listing value of ₹468.25. On the BSE, it listed at ₹580, a 24.99 per cent premium to ₹464.05. The stock then fell to the lower circuit of ₹557.65 on the NSE, where it closed. NSE data showed a high of ₹589.90, a traded volume of 10.14 lakh shares and a total market capitalisation of ₹10,761.39 crore.

Demerger scheme

The listing follows the demerger of the graphite electrodes business under a composite scheme sanctioned by the NCLT Indore Bench on August 13, 2026. The scheme took effect on September 1. Shareholders on the September 7 record date received one HEG Ltd share for each share held in HEG Advanced Materials Ltd, the renamed original entity. The scheme also merged Bhilwara Energy Ltd into HEG Advanced Materials at an 8:7 exchange ratio.

HEG Advanced Materials houses the advanced materials, battery energy solutions and green power businesses. It traded 1.80 per cent higher at ₹285.60 against a previous close of ₹280.55.

HEG Ltd operates what it calls the world’s largest single-site UHP graphite electrode facility at Mandideep, with a capacity of 100,000 tonnes a year. It exports 65–70 per cent of output to over 35 countries. The board has approved a ₹650 crore brownfield expansion to 115,000 tonnes, with production targeted for the first quarter of calendar 2028.

Aditya Birla Money Research, in a November 26 note, said the stock was not rated. It said HEG’s EBITDA per tonne was about $839 in Q2FY27 and could rise to $1,200–1,300 in FY28E as pricing contracts reset. It estimated EBITDA could reach ₹11.0-12.5 billion by FY28/29E, from an implied run rate of about ₹7.4 billion. The brokerage noted that pro forma financials for the listed entity are not yet available.
